knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)

This document is the R counterpart of the Python notebook
[Part 07 - Analyzing Visual Content](../../Notebooks/Part%2007%20-%20Analyzing%20Visual%20Content/Part%2007%20-%20Analyzing%20Visual%20Content.ipynb).

> **tl;dr**: A large share of social media communication is visual —
> photos, screenshots, memes, charts, video, and link previews — yet most
> data science tutorials stop at text. Here we measure how Bluesky
> accounts use visual media, audit alt-text accessibility practices, map
> the domains behind link cards, and build a small, responsibly collected
> image corpus.

Fifteen years of Twitter research taught us how to count words, but
platforms became steadily more visual while our methods mostly did not.
[Highfield & Leaver (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1080/22041451.2016.1155332)
argued that social media research needed a methodological toolkit for
"the visual turn" — and that building one raises new ethical questions,
because images carry faces, locations, and contexts that text does not.

Bluesky is an unusually good place to take up that challenge, for three
reasons. First, every post's media attachments are described by public,
machine-readable **embed** records — an *embed* is the structured
attachment that travels with a post (an image set, a video, a link
preview, or a quoted post), stored separately from the post's text.
Second, the image files themselves are served from an open **CDN** — a
*content delivery network*, the layer of globally distributed cache
servers that platforms use to deliver images and video quickly — so
anyone with a URL can fetch a preview-sized copy. Third, Bluesky's
interface nudges users to write **alt text**: the textual image
description that a **screen reader** (software that blind and low-vision
users rely on to speak interface content aloud or render it as braille)
reads in place of the pixels. Bluesky even offers a setting that
*requires* alt text before posting. If you have never written alt text
yourself, [WebAIM's guide to alternative text](https://webaim.org/techniques/alttext/)
is a ten-minute read that will make the middle of this document much
more concrete.

That last affordance makes Bluesky a natural follow-up to
[Gleason et al. (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3308558.3313605), who
found that when Twitter made alt text available behind an opt-in
setting, only about **0.1% of image tweets** ended up with a
description — a near-total failure of voluntary accessibility. Is
Bluesky's alt-text culture measurably different? By the end of this
document you will have an empirical answer for a small panel of
accounts, and the tools to scale the question up.

### Learning objectives

1. Distinguish the AT Protocol's embed types — `images`, `video`,
   `external` (link cards), `record` (quote posts), and
   `recordWithMedia` — and classify any post's media.
2. Understand the difference between a post's *record* embed (what the
   author wrote) and its hydrated embed *view* (what clients render), and
   why raw responses are sometimes more robust than typed models.
3. Measure how often a panel of accounts posts each kind of media.
4. Audit **alt-text provision** as a quantitative accessibility measure,
   against the Twitter baseline of Gleason et al. (2019).
5. Extract and tabulate the **domains** behind link cards to
   characterize an information ecosystem.
6. Build a small image corpus on disk — thumbnails only, content-hash
   filenames, a manifest — and display it.
7. Know how CLIP-style image embeddings extend this pipeline to
   clustering and zero-shot classification of image *content*.

## Setup

The usual packages: [bskyr](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/) for
the API, the [tidyverse](https://www.tidyverse.org/) for tables and
plots, [jsonlite](https://cran.r-project.org/package=jsonlite) for
reading saved JSON, and [lubridate](https://lubridate.tidyverse.org/)
for timestamps. Two more appear later without a `library()` call:
[digest](https://cran.r-project.org/package=digest) computes the content
hashes that name our image files, and knitr's
[`include_graphics()`](https://rdrr.io/cran/knitr/man/include_graphics.html)
displays the downloaded images.

```{r libraries}
library(bskyr)
library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)
library(lubridate)
```

As in every part of this series, the shared helper `bsky_client.R` looks
for credentials (an `atproto.json` file or bskyr's environment
variables), authenticates if it finds them, and sets `bsky_authed`. The
`knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = bsky_authed)` line then makes that flag the
default for the whole document: with credentials every chunk runs;
without them the document still knits, but the API chunks are skipped.
(The few chunks that read saved files instead of the API say
`eval = TRUE`, so they run either way.)

```{r connect}
source("bsky_client.R")
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = bsky_authed)
```

## 1. The anatomy of a Bluesky embed

When a Bluesky post carries media — a photo, a video, a preview card for
a link — the attachment does not live inside the post's text. It lives in
a separate structured field called the post's **embed**. Each kind of
embed is defined by a **lexicon**, the AT Protocol's machine-readable
schema language ([lexicon spec](https://atproto.com/specs/lexicon));
Bluesky documents them in the guide to
[post embeds](https://bsky.network/docs/advanced-guides/posts) and the
[HTTP API reference](https://endpoints.bsky.app). The protocol defines a
small family of them:

| Lexicon | What it is |
|---|---|
| `app.bsky.embed.images` | One or more attached images, each with optional **alt text** and an aspect ratio |
| `app.bsky.embed.video` | An attached video with a thumbnail |
| `app.bsky.embed.external` | A **link card**: a URL plus the title, description, and preview image scraped from it |
| `app.bsky.embed.record` | A **quote post**: a reference to another record |
| `app.bsky.embed.recordWithMedia` | A quote post *plus* attached media (images, video, or a link card) |

Each embed appears in **two places** in an API response, and the
distinction matters:

* `post$record$embed` — the raw record the **author** wrote. The image
  files themselves are not stored inside the record: they are **blobs**,
  the protocol's term for arbitrary binary files (images, video) kept on
  the author's data server ([blob spec](https://atproto.com/specs/blob)).
  The record points at each blob with a **content hash** — a short,
  unique fingerprint computed from the file's bytes, so the same file
  always yields the same hash and changing a single pixel changes it
  completely. A content hash *identifies* a file, but it is not a URL you
  can click.
* `post$embed` — the hydrated **view** that the AppView (the indexing
  server that assembles what clients display) constructs for clients.
  The view resolves blob references into ready-to-fetch CDN URLs —
  `thumb` for a small preview rendition (a **thumbnail**) and `fullsize`
  for a larger one — carries the same alt text, and marks itself with a
  `#view` suffix on its `$type` (e.g. `app.bsky.embed.images#view`).

For analysis we generally want the view — it has the URLs. With
`clean = FALSE`,
[`bs_get_author_feed()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_author_feed.html)
returns the response exactly as the server sent it: a list of pages,
each holding a `feed` list of items, each item holding a `post`. Here
are the embed types on one page of the official account's feed:

```{r raw-page}
page <- bs_get_author_feed("bsky.app", limit = 30, clean = FALSE)

items <- page[[1]]$feed

map_chr(items, \(item) item$post$embed$`$type` %||% "(no embed)") |>
  table()
```

A classifier collapses those view types into analytic classes, and
shunts anything it has never seen into `"other"` instead of crashing.
`app.bsky.embed.gallery`, a multi-photo carousel Bluesky shipped in
2025, is a set of photos, so for analysis it counts as `"images"`:

```{r classify, eval=TRUE}
classify_embed <- function(post) {
  type <- post$embed$`$type` %||% return("none")
  type <- sub("#view$", "", type)
  switch(type,
    "app.bsky.embed.images" = "images",
    "app.bsky.embed.gallery" = "images",   # multi-photo carousel
    "app.bsky.embed.video" = "video",
    "app.bsky.embed.external" = "external",
    "app.bsky.embed.record" = "record",
    "app.bsky.embed.recordWithMedia" = "record_with_media",
    "other")
}
```

### When typed models meet a platform in flux

There is a practical wrinkle. Embed lexicons are the fastest-moving part
of the protocol, and code that expects a fixed set of shapes breaks when
the platform ships a new one. Python's atproto SDK validates every
response against typed models, and for a while galleries appeared in
feeds before the SDK could model them: earlier versions of the Python
notebook crashed on the very first `bsky.app` page. Whether a live page
trips anything on the day you run this depends on what the platform
shipped, so both notebooks teach the lesson on a saved page instead.

`embed_drift_fixture.json`, saved in the Python part's `data/` folder,
holds three real posts from `bsky.app`'s feed with two deliberate edits
(recorded in `embed_drift_fixture_metadata.json` next to it):

1. **A known embed type whose shape changed.** In one
   `app.bsky.embed.images#view` embed, each image's `thumb` field has
   been renamed `previewUrl`, the kind of change a new lexicon version
   can bring.
2. **A brand-new embed type.** Another post carries a made-up
   `app.bsky.embed.hologram#view` embed that no software has ever
   modeled.

R's lists never fail validation, because nothing validates them. But
that only moves the problem into our own code. Watch what the
classifier and a naive field lookup make of the two edits:

```{r drift-fixture, eval=TRUE}
FIXTURE <- file.path("..", "..", "Notebooks", "Part 07 - Analyzing Visual Content",
                     "data", "embed_drift_fixture.json")
drift_page <- read_json(FIXTURE)

tibble(
  post = seq_along(drift_page$feed),
  embed_type = map_chr(drift_page$feed, \(item) item$post$embed$`$type`),
  class = map_chr(drift_page$feed, \(item) classify_embed(item$post)),
  # for posts with images: the fields the first image carries, and its thumb URL
  image_fields = map_chr(drift_page$feed, \(item) {
    img <- item$post$embed$images[[1]]
    if (is.null(img)) "(no images)" else paste(names(img), collapse = ", ")
  }),
  thumb = map_chr(drift_page$feed, \(item) {
    img <- item$post$embed$images[[1]]
    if (is.null(img)) "(no images)" else img$thumb %||% NA_character_
  })
)
```

The made-up type lands in `"other"`, which is the classifier doing its
job: we can count unknown types and go look at them. The renamed field
is quieter and more dangerous. The images post still classifies as
`images`, but its thumbnail URL comes back `NA`, so an analysis that
downloads thumbnails would silently skip it. In Python the same edit is
fatal in the other direction: the SDK rejects the whole page with a
validation error, losing every post on it. Neither failure is a bug so
much as a fact of life on an actively evolving protocol — one of the
reproducibility hazards flagged back in Part 01. Nor is it confined to
embeds: in 2026 Bluesky's moderation service stopped accepting the
wildcard label queries an earlier version of Part 09 relied on. Same
code, same endpoint, different answer. The defensive habits are always
the same: save raw responses, check what came back, and count the cases
your code doesn't recognize rather than letting them vanish.

## 2. Collecting a media panel

To say anything about media *practices* we need a **panel**: a fixed set
of accounts whose posts we observe, so that differences between
accounts, rather than a jumble of one-off posts, become the unit of
analysis. Following this series' conventions we start from the two
standing example accounts — `bsky.app` (the official platform account)
and `nytimes.com` (The New York Times) — and add organizational accounts
with contrasting communication styles.

How do we find those? When a post mentions another account
("@someone"), the mention is recorded in the post's `facets`, the
structured annotations over a post's text that we met in Part 02 (see
the [rich text guide](https://bsky.network/docs/advanced-guides/post-richtext)).
A mention facet stores the mentioned account's **DID** (decentralized
identifier — the stable, machine-readable ID behind a handle, which never
changes even when the handle does). As a discovery demo, we page through
about 500 of `nytimes.com`'s recent posts, count mention DIDs, and
resolve the most frequent ones back to handles with
[`bs_get_profile()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_profile.html):

```{r mentions}
mention_pages <- bs_get_author_feed("nytimes.com", limit = 500, clean = FALSE)
mention_items <- list_flatten(map(mention_pages, "feed"))

mention_dids <- map(mention_items, \(item) {
  map(item$post$record$facets %||% list(), \(facet) {
    mentions <- keep(facet$features, \(f) endsWith(f$`$type`, "#mention"))
    map_chr(mentions, "did")
  })
}) |> unlist()

top_mentioned <- head(sort(table(mention_dids), decreasing = TRUE), 8)
bs_get_profile(names(top_mentioned)) |>
  select(did, handle, display_name) |>
  mutate(mentions = as.integer(top_mentioned[did])) |>
  arrange(desc(mentions))
```

The accounts a newsroom mentions most turn out to be its own sister
accounts and journalists — useful for seeing how the discovery technique
works, but a panel built only from them would be six flavors of the same
institution. So we hand-pick instead: organizational accounts with
contrasting communication styles (organizations post a lot of media, and
studying organizations rather than private individuals is the ethically
conservative choice — more on this at the end). Our panel is the two
standing accounts plus four more: a public broadcaster, a nonprofit
local newsroom, an investigative newsroom, and a policy institute.

The collector below fetches each account's feed as raw pages, flattens
the pages together, uses
[`purrr::keep()`](https://purrr.tidyverse.org/reference/keep.html) to
retain only original posts, and extracts the `post` object from each
item. "Original" means two things here, matching the Python notebook. We
skip **reposts** (a feed item whose `reason` says it was reposted),
because a repost shows someone else's media choices and we want to
attribute practices like alt-text provision to the account that actually
made them. And we skip **replies**, because we want each account's
primary, public-facing output rather than its conversations. The Python
notebook gets the second for free by asking the API for
`filter = "posts_no_replies"`; bskyr's `bs_get_author_feed()` has no
`filter` argument, so we drop replies ourselves, by checking whether the
post's record points to a parent. That costs a little: the API still
sends the replies, so each account yields somewhat fewer than
`POSTS_PER_ACCOUNT` original posts:

```{r panel}
PANEL <- c("bsky.app", "npr.org", "boulderrl.bsky.social",
           "propublica.org", "nytimes.com", "knightcolumbia.org")
POSTS_PER_ACCOUNT <- 135
COLLECTED_AT <- format(now("UTC"), "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")

collect_raw_posts <- function(actor, max_posts) {
  pages <- bs_get_author_feed(actor, limit = max_posts, clean = FALSE)
  items <- list_flatten(map(pages, "feed"))
  originals <- keep(items, \(item) {
    repost <- endsWith(item$reason$`$type` %||% "", "#reasonRepost")
    reply <- !is.null(item$post$record$reply)   # the record names a parent post
    !repost && !reply
  })
  map(originals, "post")
}

all_posts <- map(PANEL, \(actor) {
  posts <- collect_raw_posts(actor, POSTS_PER_ACCOUNT)
  Sys.sleep(0.1)
  posts
}) |> set_names(PANEL)

map_int(all_posts, length)
```

Both collection decisions — no reposts, no replies — shape every number
below, so we record them in the metadata file we save at the end. When a
collection decision changes your numbers, future-you (and your readers)
need to be able to find it.

Now three helpers that walk a raw post. `iter_images()` returns one row
per attached image, with its alt text and declared dimensions. It has to
look in three places, because the image list lives in different spots
for plain image posts (`embed$images`, with a `thumb` URL per image),
galleries (`embed$items`, with a `thumbnail` URL per image), and posts
that pair media with a quote (`embed$media`, which holds one of the
other two). `external_info()` pulls the link card and reduces its URL to
a bare domain with a regular expression. `post_row()` assembles
everything into the one-row-per-post summary our analysis runs on:

```{r media-helpers}
iter_images <- function(post) {
  view <- post$embed
  if (startsWith(view$`$type` %||% "", "app.bsky.embed.recordWithMedia")) {
    view <- view$media
  }
  imgs <- view$images %||% view$items %||% list()   # images or gallery
  # a post with no images still returns a (zero-row) tibble with the columns,
  # so code downstream can filter and count without special cases
  if (length(imgs) == 0) {
    return(tibble(alt = character(), thumb = character(),
                  width = integer(), height = integer()))
  }
  map(imgs, \(img) tibble(
    alt = img$alt %||% "",
    thumb = img$thumb %||% img$thumbnail %||% NA_character_,
    width = img$aspectRatio$width %||% NA_integer_,
    height = img$aspectRatio$height %||% NA_integer_
  )) |> list_rbind()
}

url_domain <- function(url) {
  str_to_lower(str_match(url, "^https?://(?:www\\.)?([^/]+)")[, 2])
}

external_info <- function(post) {
  ext <- post$embed$external
  if (is.null(ext)) return(NULL)
  tibble(title = ext$title %||% "",
         domain = url_domain(ext$uri %||% ""))
}

post_row <- function(post) {
  imgs <- iter_images(post)
  ext <- external_info(post)
  tibble(
    uri = post$uri,
    author = post$author$handle,
    created_at = post$record$createdAt %||% NA_character_,
    embed_class = classify_embed(post),
    n_images = nrow(imgs),
    n_images_with_alt = sum(str_squish(imgs$alt) != ""),
    external_domain = if (is.null(ext)) NA_character_ else ext$domain
  )
}

df <- map(all_posts, \(posts) map(posts, post_row) |> list_rbind()) |>
  list_rbind()

cat(nrow(df), "posts from", n_distinct(df$author), "accounts\n")
count(df, embed_class, sort = TRUE)
```

### A worked example of each embed type

Before aggregating, let's look at one real example of every embed class
the panel produced, to connect the abstract type names to actual posts.
As you read each example, match it back to the lexicon table in Section
1: an `images` post carries alt text, a `video` post carries a thumbnail
URL and an aspect ratio, an `external` post carries a domain and a
scraped title, and the two `record` flavors point at another post.
(Because this runs against the live network, the specific posts — and
even which classes appear — will differ each time you run it.)

```{r worked-examples}
describe_embed <- function(post) {
  text <- str_squish(post$record$text %||% "")
  view <- post$embed %||% list()
  view_type <- view$`$type` %||% "(no embed view)"
  cat("  @", post$author$handle, ': "', str_trunc(text, 80), '"\n', sep = "")
  cat("  view $type:", view_type, "\n")
  imgs <- iter_images(post)
  if (nrow(imgs) > 0) {
    first_alt <- if (nzchar(str_squish(imgs$alt[1]))) str_trunc(imgs$alt[1], 60) else "(none)"
    cat("  ", nrow(imgs), " image(s); first alt text: ", first_alt, "\n", sep = "")
  }
  if (startsWith(view_type, "app.bsky.embed.video")) {
    cat("  aspect ratio:", view$aspectRatio$width %||% "?", "x",
        view$aspectRatio$height %||% "?", "\n")
  }
  card <- external_info(post)
  if (!is.null(card)) cat("  link card ->", card$domain, ":", str_trunc(card$title, 60), "\n")
  if (str_detect(view_type, "^app\\.bsky\\.embed\\.record(#|WithMedia)")) {
    quoted <- view$record$record %||% view$record   # recordWithMedia nests one level deeper
    cat("  quotes a post by @", quoted$author$handle %||% "(unavailable)", "\n", sep = "")
  }
}

flat_posts <- list_flatten(unname(all_posts))
classes <- map_chr(flat_posts, classify_embed)
for (embed_class in c("images", "video", "external", "record", "record_with_media", "none")) {
  hit <- which(classes == embed_class)
  if (length(hit) == 0) next
  cat("---", embed_class, "\n")
  describe_embed(flat_posts[[hit[1]]])
}
```

## 3. How visual is the panel?

The most basic descriptive question: what fraction of posts carry each
kind of embed? We count posts by class and divide by the total, so the
bars are shares that sum to 1:

```{r embed-shares, fig.width=8, fig.height=4}
EMBED_ORDER <- c("external", "images", "video", "record", "record_with_media", "none", "other")

df |>
  count(embed_class) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n),
         embed_class = factor(embed_class, levels = EMBED_ORDER)) |>
  ggplot(aes(embed_class, share)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", share)), vjust = -0.3, size = 3) +
  labs(x = "Embed type", y = "Share of posts",
       title = paste("Embed types across", nrow(df), "panel posts")) +
  theme_minimal()
```

On this panel, posts with **no** embed — pure text — are a minority. But
the overall bar hides enormous differences between accounts, which is
the real finding. To see them we compute each account's *composition*:
the share of its posts in each class, so that accounts posting at
different volumes are directly comparable. A table and a stacked bar
show the same numbers two ways:

```{r composition, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.5}
by_account <- df |>
  count(author, embed_class) |>
  group_by(author) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup()

by_account |>
  select(-n) |>
  mutate(share = round(share, 2),
         embed_class = factor(embed_class, levels = EMBED_ORDER)) |>
  arrange(embed_class) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = embed_class, values_from = share, values_fill = 0) |>
  arrange(match(author, PANEL))

by_account |>
  mutate(author = factor(author, levels = rev(PANEL)),
         embed_class = factor(embed_class, levels = EMBED_ORDER)) |>
  ggplot(aes(share, author, fill = embed_class)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Share of posts", y = NULL, fill = "Embed type",
       title = "Embed type composition by account") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Each account has a visual *signature*. The news organizations are
link-card machines — most of their posts exist to push readers to
articles on their own websites. The platform account mixes announcement
screenshots, videos, and quote posts. The policy institute pairs its
link cards with a noticeable share of its own video and images. Check
these descriptions against the table above from your own run: the exact
shares move from run to run, but each account's signature is usually
stable. These signatures are themselves data: an account's embed mix
encodes its communicative role.

### Images per post and aspect ratios

For posts that carry images (including the image half of
`recordWithMedia` embeds), how many do they attach, and what shapes are
they? An image's **aspect ratio** is its width divided by its height:
values above 1 are landscape (wider than tall), values below 1 are
portrait (taller than wide), and exactly 1 is square. The embed view's
`aspectRatio` field reports width and height in the metadata, which means
we can study image *shape* without downloading a single pixel.

```{r images-per-post}
images_df <- imap(all_posts, \(posts, actor) {
  map(posts, iter_images) |> list_rbind() |> mutate(author = actor)
}) |> list_rbind()

image_posts <- df |> filter(n_images > 0)
cat(nrow(image_posts), "posts carry", nrow(images_df), "images (",
    round(mean(image_posts$n_images), 2), "images per image-post )\n")
count(image_posts, n_images)
```

The histogram below shows the distribution of aspect ratios, with dashed
reference lines at three culturally meaningful shapes: 9:16 (a phone held
upright — most phone photos and app screenshots), 1:1 (square — the
classic designed social-media card), and 16:9 (a widescreen monitor or
video frame). One wrinkle to anticipate: `aspectRatio` is an *optional*
field in the lexicon, so some images simply do not report it. We drop
those rows and say how many we dropped in the plot title — silently
discarding data is how analyses quietly go wrong.

```{r aspect, fig.width=8, fig.height=4}
with_ratio <- images_df |>
  filter(!is.na(width), !is.na(height)) |>
  mutate(aspect = width / height)

ggplot(with_ratio, aes(aspect)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(9 / 16, 1, 16 / 9),
             color = "#DC143C", linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = c(9 / 16, 1, 16 / 9), y = Inf, vjust = 1.5, size = 3,
           color = "#DC143C", label = c("9:16", "1:1", "16:9")) +
  labs(x = "Aspect ratio (width / height)", y = "Images",
       title = paste0("Aspect ratios of ", nrow(with_ratio), " images (",
                      nrow(images_df) - nrow(with_ratio), " without aspectRatio dropped)")) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Aspect ratios are a cheap, download-free proxy for image *genre*: spikes
near 16:9 usually mean screenshots, video stills, and link-preview
graphics; 1:1 suggests designed social cards and profile-style photos;
tall portrait ratios suggest phone photos and screenshots of other apps.
A content analysis would verify those guesses against the pixels — which
is exactly what Sections 6 and 7 set up.

## 4. Alt text: accessibility as a measurable practice

This is the centerpiece of the document. **Alt text** is the description
a sighted author writes so that blind and low-vision users, whose screen
readers cannot interpret pixels, get the content of an image. Good alt
text conveys the image's *function and content* in context — "Line chart
showing Bluesky signups spiking after the November announcement" rather
than "chart" — and [WebAIM's alt-text guidance](https://webaim.org/techniques/alttext/)
is the standard accessible reference on what that means in practice.
Whether authors actually write it is a concrete, countable behavioral
measure of how much a community's accessibility norms are worth.

The Twitter baseline is grim. Gleason et al. (2019) audited 1.09 million
image tweets and found that only **0.1%** had alt text — even though
Twitter had offered the feature since 2016 — because it was buried behind
an opt-in setting that almost nobody enabled. Their title quotes a
frustrated screen-reader user: *"It's almost like they're trying to hide
it."*

Bluesky made different design choices: the alt-text field is visible by
default in the posting interface, images without descriptions are
badged in some clients, and a
[user setting](https://bsky.app/settings/accessibility) can **require**
alt text before a post will send. Did the design choices and the
community norms that grew around them move the number? We compute three
related rates, because they answer slightly different questions: the
share of *image posts* where **all** images are described (the strictest
standard — a screen-reader user gets the whole post), the share where
**any** image is described, and the share of *individual images* with a
description (the number most directly comparable to Gleason et al.):

```{r alt-rates}
# (the first column is n_image_posts, not image_posts: tibble() builds
# columns in order, so a column named image_posts would hide the data frame)
tibble(
  n_image_posts = nrow(image_posts),
  all_images_described = mean(image_posts$n_images_with_alt ==
                              image_posts$n_images),
  any_image_described = mean(image_posts$n_images_with_alt > 0),
  n_images = nrow(images_df),
  images_with_alt = mean(str_squish(images_df$alt) != ""),
  twitter_2019_baseline = 0.001
)
```

Orders of magnitude above the Twitter baseline — even the
*lowest-provision* account in this panel will typically beat 0.1% by an
order of magnitude or more. But provision is far from uniform: it is a
per-account practice, so let's measure it per account. One detail
matters: an account that posted *no* images in our sample has no
alt-text rate at all. Zero described images out of zero is undefined, not
0%, so we name those accounts rather than plotting them as zeros or
letting them silently drop off the chart:

```{r alt-by-account, fig.width=8, fig.height=4}
alt_by_account <- images_df |>
  group_by(author) |>
  summarise(images = n(),
            alt_rate = mean(str_squish(alt) != ""))

no_images <- setdiff(PANEL, alt_by_account$author)
if (length(no_images) > 0) {
  cat("No images in the sample, so no alt-text rate:",
      paste(no_images, collapse = ", "), "\n")
}

alt_by_account |>
  ggplot(aes(alt_rate, fct_reorder(author, alt_rate))) +
  geom_col(fill = "seagreen") +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(scales::percent(alt_rate, 1), " (n=", images, ")")),
            hjust = -0.1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.001, color = "#DC143C", linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1.15)) +
  labs(x = "Share of posted images with alt text", y = NULL,
       title = "Alt-text provision rate by account (accounts that posted images)",
       subtitle = "Dashed red line: Twitter 2019 baseline (0.1%)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Treat the per-account rates with appropriate humility: some accounts
post few images, so their rates have wide error bars, and an account
listed above as having no images tells us nothing about its alt-text
practice either way. Link-card-only newsrooms often land on that list,
because their posts carry a link preview instead of an uploaded image.
Still, the pattern is informative. Accounts embedded in Bluesky's
early-adopter culture (where "no alt text, no repost" is a common stated
norm) describe nearly everything; organizational accounts that
cross-post from other platforms via scheduling tools often describe much
less, because the tooling, not the platform, sets the default.

### How much do people write?

Provision is binary; *quality* is not. Description length is a crude but
useful first proxy — a five-word alt text and a five-sentence one are
very different accessibility experiences.

```{r alt-length, fig.width=8, fig.height=4}
alt_lengths <- images_df |>
  filter(str_squish(alt) != "") |>
  mutate(alt_len = nchar(alt))

ggplot(alt_lengths, aes(alt_len)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "seagreen", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median(alt_lengths$alt_len),
             linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Alt text length (characters)", y = "Images",
       title = paste("Length of", nrow(alt_lengths), "non-empty alt texts"),
       subtitle = paste("Dashed line: median =", median(alt_lengths$alt_len), "characters")) +
  theme_minimal()

summary(alt_lengths$alt_len)
```

Summary statistics flatten a lot. To get a feel for what these
descriptions actually *are*, let's read two real ones — the shortest and
the longest in the panel. Watching the extremes is a good habit with any
text field: the shortest values reveal perfunctory compliance (a single
word, a stray character), while the longest reveal what dedicated
describers are doing with the space.

```{r alt-extremes}
bind_rows(
  slice_min(alt_lengths, alt_len, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |> mutate(which = "Shortest"),
  slice_max(alt_lengths, alt_len, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |> mutate(which = "Longest")
) |>
  transmute(which, author, alt_len, alt = str_trunc(str_squish(alt), 300))
```

Note that many alt texts are longer than the 300-character post limit —
Bluesky allows up to 2,000 characters of alt text, and people use them.
Some of the longest "alt texts" in the wild are full transcriptions of
screenshotted documents, which serves screen-reader users and,
incidentally, makes the *image's* content searchable and analyzable as
text. For a researcher, alt text is a gift twice over: it is an
accessibility measure, *and* it is a free, author-written caption corpus
for the multimodal analyses in Section 7.

The research framing matters here. Gleason et al. were not just
counting; they showed that a **design choice** (hiding the feature)
produced a **population-level accessibility failure**. Bluesky's
contrasting choices — visible field, optional enforcement, community
norms — constitute a natural comparison. A full study would sample
accounts systematically (not a six-account convenience panel), track
provision over account tenure (do newcomers learn the norm?), and compare
across communities on the same platform.

## 5. Link cards: who points where?

`external` embeds — link cards — are the connective tissue between
Bluesky and the rest of the web. Every card carries the destination URL,
so we can extract each URL's **domain** (the `nytimes.com` part) and
ask: which websites does this panel's attention point to?
`external_info()` already reduced every card's URL to a lowercased
domain with any leading `www.` stripped, so `www.NYTimes.com` and
`nytimes.com` count as the same place. We tabulate the ten most-linked
domains and each one's share of all link cards:

```{r domains}
external_posts <- df |> filter(!is.na(external_domain))
cat(nrow(external_posts), "posts with link cards across",
    n_distinct(external_posts$external_domain), "distinct domains\n")

external_posts |>
  count(external_domain, sort = TRUE, name = "link_cards") |>
  mutate(share = round(link_cards / nrow(external_posts), 3)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)
```

The top-domains table answers "where does the panel point?" A sharper
question is how much of each account's link sharing is
**self-linking**: cards that point back to the account's own website. On
Bluesky, organizations typically use their web domain *as their handle*
(`propublica.org` the account posts links to `propublica.org` the
website), but the mapping is not always one-to-one. The Boulder
Reporting Lab's handle is `boulderrl.bsky.social` but its site is
`boulderreportinglab.org`, and several newsrooms post through **link
shorteners**, short domains that redirect to their articles: NPR uses
`n.pr`, the New York Times `nyti.ms`, and ProPublica `propub.li`. A
shortened link to an NPR story is still NPR linking to itself, so each
shortener counts as one of its outlet's own domains. `is_own_domain()`
accepts a domain if it equals one of the account's domains or is a
subdomain of one (so `projects.propublica.org` counts, but a stranger's
`notnpr.org` does not):

```{r self-links}
OWN_DOMAINS <- list(
  "bsky.app" = c("bsky.app", "bsky.social"),
  "npr.org" = c("npr.org", "n.pr"),
  "boulderrl.bsky.social" = "boulderreportinglab.org",
  "propublica.org" = c("propublica.org", "propub.li"),
  "nytimes.com" = c("nytimes.com", "nyti.ms"),
  "knightcolumbia.org" = "knightcolumbia.org"
)

is_own_domain <- function(domain, own) {
  any(domain == own | endsWith(domain, paste0(".", own)))
}

external_posts <- external_posts |>
  mutate(own_domain = map2_lgl(external_domain, author,
                               \(d, a) is_own_domain(d, OWN_DOMAINS[[a]])))

# For each account, the most common destination we did NOT count as its
# own: a shortener or subdomain here means OWN_DOMAINS needs fixing
top_other <- external_posts |>
  filter(!own_domain) |>
  count(author, external_domain, sort = TRUE) |>
  group_by(author) |>
  slice_head(n = 1) |>
  select(author, top_other_domain = external_domain)

external_posts |>
  group_by(author) |>
  summarise(link_cards = n(), own_domain_share = round(mean(own_domain), 2)) |>
  left_join(top_other, by = "author")
```

The top-10 table is dominated by the panel members' own websites and
their shorteners, a reminder that domain analysis always has to contend
with shorteners and redirectors. Matching on the bare website domain
alone would score NPR, whose cards almost all point to `n.pr`, as never
linking to itself, and the conclusion would be exactly backwards. The
`top_other_domain` column is the check that catches this kind of
mistake. When it shows a shortener or subdomain, fix `OWN_DOMAINS`; when
it shows other outlets or platforms (video sites, partner newsrooms),
the account really is pointing outward. One case needs more care:
`trib.al` and similar shorteners belong to social-media scheduling
services that many outlets share, so they can't be assigned to any one
account. The only way to know where such a link goes is to follow its
redirect (for example with `httr2::req_perform()` on the URL and reading
the final `httr2::resp_url()`) and record the final domain. At scale that
means one extra request per link, so budget for it.

Read the shares with that in mind. For the news organizations, Bluesky
typically works overwhelmingly as a *distribution channel* for their own
publishing, with own-domain shares near 1. The platform account and the
policy institute usually link to a broader ecosystem of other sites.

This is a miniature of a classic research design. Link-sharing graphs
were how Twitter researchers mapped media ecosystems, measured the
prevalence of low-credibility sources, and traced how news circulates
between outlets and audiences. On Bluesky, every link card in every
public post is collectable the same way we just did — no special API
tier required. Scaled to thousands of accounts, the domain table becomes
a bipartite account–domain network ripe for the methods of Part 03.

## 6. Building a small image corpus

So far we have analyzed *metadata about* images. To analyze the images
themselves we need pixels on disk. We build a *small*, documented corpus
following habits worth copying for any image collection:

1. **Thumbnails, not full-size blobs.** The embed view's `thumb` URL
   serves a CDN-resized preview rendition — a small, reduced-resolution
   copy generated by the platform for fast display. For most
   computational analyses (and certainly for CLIP, which sees 224×224
   pixels) thumbnails are sufficient; full-size downloads waste bandwidth
   and multiply the sensitivity of what you are storing.
2. **Content-hash filenames.** Each file is named by a hash of its bytes
   (the first 16 characters of its SHA-256 digest, computed with
   [`digest::digest()`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=digest)) — the
   same content-hash idea the protocol itself uses for blobs (Section 1).
   Identical bytes always get the same name, so the same image posted
   twice is saved once, and re-running never duplicates files.
3. **A manifest.** Pixels without provenance are useless; every saved
   file gets a row recording its post, author, alt text, and dimensions,
   so any image can be traced back to the post it came from. The
   manifest, not the folder, defines the corpus, so we empty the folder
   first: images left over from an earlier run would otherwise sneak into
   any analysis that reads it.
4. **A diverse, capped sample.** At most 12 images and 2 per post, taken
   round-robin across accounts with alt-texted posts first, so one
   prolific image-poster can't dominate.
5. **Politeness.** Half a second between downloads, just as we sleep
   between API pages.

One difference from Python: the Python notebook also shrinks every
thumbnail to at most 256 pixels on a side before saving. Base R can't
resize images, and this series avoids adding an image-processing package
for one step, so here the CDN's thumbnail is saved as-is (still small,
typically tens of kilobytes).

```{r download}
MAX_IMAGES <- 12
MAX_PER_POST <- 2
dir.create("data/images", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
unlink(list.files("data/images", pattern = "\\.jpg$", full.names = TRUE))

# Candidate images: up to MAX_PER_POST per post, alt-texted posts first
candidates <- imap(all_posts, \(posts, actor) {
  map(posts, \(post) {
    imgs <- iter_images(post) |> filter(!is.na(thumb))
    if (nrow(imgs) == 0) return(NULL)
    imgs |>
      slice_head(n = MAX_PER_POST) |>
      mutate(author = actor, uri = post$uri,
             post_has_alt = any(str_squish(alt) != ""))
  }) |> list_rbind()
}) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  arrange(author, desc(post_has_alt)) |>
  group_by(author) |>
  mutate(turn = dense_rank(match(uri, unique(uri)))) |>  # 1st post, 2nd post, ...
  ungroup() |>
  arrange(turn, match(author, PANEL))                    # round-robin

# Download until the corpus is full, naming each file by its content hash
manifest <- list()
for (i in seq_len(nrow(candidates))) {
  if (length(manifest) >= MAX_IMAGES) break
  tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".jpg")
  ok <- tryCatch(download.file(candidates$thumb[i], tmp, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE) == 0,
                 error = \(e) FALSE)
  Sys.sleep(0.5)
  if (!ok) next
  hash <- substr(digest::digest(file = tmp, algo = "sha256"), 1, 16)
  dest <- file.path("data/images", paste0(hash, ".jpg"))
  if (file.exists(dest)) next                            # same image already saved
  file.copy(tmp, dest)
  manifest[[length(manifest) + 1]] <- candidates[i, ] |>
    select(author, uri, alt, width, height) |>
    mutate(file = dest)
}
manifest <- list_rbind(manifest)

write_csv(manifest, "data/images_manifest.csv")

c(images_saved = nrow(manifest),
  total_kb = round(sum(file.size(manifest$file)) / 1024))
```

Now display the corpus as a grid, using each image's **alt text as its
description** in the rendered page. knitr's `include_graphics()` places
the files side by side, and the chunk option `fig.alt` attaches each
image's author-written alt text to it, so a screen-reader user reading
this document hears the same descriptions the authors wrote. This is a
habit worth keeping for two reasons: it keeps the author's own
description attached to the pixels as the corpus travels through your
analysis, and it makes images that travel with *no* description
instantly visible — the accessibility audit of Section 4, now as a
picture. (We label those "no alt text" rather than leaving them blank.)

```{r corpus-grid, out.width="24%", fig.show="hold", fig.alt=if (exists("manifest") && is.data.frame(manifest) && nrow(manifest) > 0) ifelse(str_squish(manifest$alt) == "", paste0("@", manifest$author, ": image with no alt text"), paste0("@", manifest$author, ": ", str_squish(manifest$alt))) else NULL}
knitr::include_graphics(manifest$file)
```

## 7. From pixels to measurements: CLIP embeddings

Twelve images you can eyeball. Twelve thousand you cannot — at that scale
you need a model that turns each image into numbers that preserve its
meaning. An **embedding** is exactly that: a vector (here, 512 numbers)
positioned so that similar things sit near each other and dissimilar
things sit far apart — the same idea as the text embeddings of Part 06,
now for pixels. The standard tool is **CLIP**
([Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020);
Radford et al. 2021): a pair of neural networks, one for images and one
for text, trained on hundreds of millions of caption–image pairs so that
an image and a text describing it land near each other in the *same*
embedding space.

That shared space buys you three analyses for free:

* **Clustering**: embed every image, run k-means on the vectors, and
  discover the corpus's visual genres (screenshots vs. photos vs. charts
  vs. memes) without labeling anything.
* **Zero-shot classification**: embed candidate labels as text ("a
  photograph of a crowd", "a screenshot of a social media post", "a data
  visualization") and assign each image the label it is most similar to —
  a classifier with no training data, just a codebook. ("Zero-shot" means
  the model has seen zero examples of your specific labels.)
* **Text–image agreement**: embed the post's text (or its alt text) and
  the image, and measure their cosine similarity — a direct
  operationalization of the multimodal question "does the image show what
  the words say?"

CLIP models are distributed as Python packages, so from R the route is
[reticulate](https://rstudio.github.io/reticulate/), which calls Python
code from R, plus the `sentence-transformers` Python package. The Python
notebook runs this workflow natively and prints a zero-shot label for
every image in its corpus. The chunk below is the same pipeline in R; it
is not evaluated when this document is knit (`eval = FALSE`), because
PyTorch, CLIP's dependency, is a large install:

```{r clip, eval=FALSE}
library(reticulate)
st <- import("sentence_transformers")
pil <- import("PIL.Image")
model <- st$SentenceTransformer("clip-ViT-B-32")

# Read the corpus from the manifest, not by listing the folder
images <- map(manifest$file, \(f) pil$open(f))
image_embeddings <- model$encode(images)

labels <- c("a screenshot of text or a user interface",
            "a photograph of one or more people",
            "a chart, map, or data visualization",
            "a logo or promotional graphic",
            "an outdoor scene or landscape")
label_embeddings <- model$encode(labels)

# Cosine similarity between every image and every label
similarity <- st$util$cos_sim(image_embeddings, label_embeddings)$numpy()
tibble(file = basename(manifest$file),
       label = labels[max.col(similarity)],
       cosine = round(apply(similarity, 1, max), 2))
```

With embeddings in hand, **visual framing analysis** becomes tractable.
Framing research asks not *whether* a topic is covered but *how it is
shown*: is a protest depicted as a crowd exercising voice or as a
confrontation with police? Is a politician photographed at a podium or
in an unflattering candid? Are climate stories illustrated with polar
bears or with flooded homes? Each of those contrasts is a pair of
zero-shot labels away. The validation discipline from Part 06 applies
with full force — you must hand-check a sample of CLIP's assignments
against human judgment before trusting any prevalence estimate, and CLIP
inherits the biases of its web-scraped training data, including
documented disparities in how it represents people across demographic
groups.

## 8. Saving and reloading the archive

Per this series' reproducibility conventions, we save the per-post
classification table, the image manifest (already written in Section 6),
and a metadata file recording when and how we collected — the panel, the
post cap, the repost and reply exclusions, and the endpoint. Every
number in this document depends on those choices: anyone re-running the
analysis (including you, six months from now) needs them to interpret,
reproduce, or fairly criticize the results.

```{r save}
write_csv(df, "data/media_summary.csv")
write_json(
  list(collected_at = COLLECTED_AT, panel = PANEL,
       posts_per_account = POSTS_PER_ACCOUNT, reposts_excluded = TRUE,
       replies_excluded = TRUE,
       endpoint = "app.bsky.feed.getAuthorFeed (raw lists via bskyr, clean = FALSE)"),
  "data/collection_metadata.json", pretty = TRUE, auto_unbox = TRUE)
```

As a final check, we prove the round trip works: reload the table from
disk and recompute a headline number without touching the network.
Downstream analyses — and your readers — should be able to start from
`data/` alone.

```{r reload}
reloaded <- read_csv("data/media_summary.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
reloaded_images <- filter(reloaded, n_images > 0)

cat("Reloaded", nrow(reloaded), "posts from data/media_summary.csv\n")
cat("Alt-text provision among image posts (all images described):",
    scales::percent(mean(reloaded_images$n_images_with_alt == reloaded_images$n_images), 0.1), "\n")
count(reloaded, embed_class, sort = TRUE)
```

## Ethics and limitations

**Images are categorically more sensitive than text.** A post's words
expose what someone chose to say; its photos can expose faces (the
author's and bystanders'), legible street signs and license plates, home
interiors, children, and contextual details the author never consciously
chose to share. Highfield & Leaver (2016) flag exactly this: visual
methods inherit all of text's ethical problems and add re-identification
of *third parties who never posted anything*. Practices this document
deliberately models, and that you should keep when scaling up:

* **Minimization.** We analyzed metadata (embed types, alt-text presence,
  aspect ratios, domains) wherever metadata sufficed, and downloaded
  pixels only for a 12-image demonstration corpus — thumbnails, not
  full-size blobs. Collect images only when your research question
  genuinely requires pixels, at the lowest resolution that answers it.
* **Public organizations over private individuals.** Our panel is
  organizational accounts plus the series' standing examples. Do not
  assemble face corpora of private individuals from their feeds, and
  never run face recognition on them; many such uses are unethical and,
  in several jurisdictions, illegal.
* **Deletion and withdrawal.** A saved image outlives the author's
  ability to delete it. Record collection dates (we did, in
  `collection_metadata.json`), re-check post existence before
  republishing any image, and treat image corpora as more
  deletion-sensitive than text archives.
* **Alt text is user data too.** Descriptions can contain names and
  contextual details; the same quoting cautions from earlier parts apply.
  And alt text is written *for* blind and low-vision users: treating it
  as research data should not crowd out that purpose.

**Limitations** to carry into any write-up: this six-account convenience
panel measures nothing about Bluesky overall — it demonstrates a method,
and its alt-text rates are certainly inflated relative to the full
network (early adopters with strong norms, organizational accounts).
Bluesky's user base is itself unrepresentative of any general
population. Embed lexicons evolve (Section 1's saved page shows how a
changed field and a new type each slip past code written for yesterday's
shapes), so classifiers need maintenance and saved raw responses. CDN
thumbnails are re-encoded renditions, not the original blobs, which
matters for forensic analyses. And CLIP-style models carry documented
demographic and cultural biases that propagate directly into any
measurement built on them.

## Exercises

These extend the document in roughly increasing order of effort.

1. **Swap the panel.** Replace the four organizational accounts in
   `PANEL` with accounts from a community you know — sports media,
   scientists, artists — and update `OWN_DOMAINS` to match (remember that
   a handle and a website domain are not always the same, as with
   `boulderrl.bsky.social`). Re-run Sections 2–5: which findings
   replicate, and which were specific to news organizations?
2. **Grow the image corpus.** Raise `MAX_IMAGES` in Section 6 to 24 and
   re-knit. Watch the printed KB total: thumbnails average roughly
   10–40 KB each, so keep an eye on how quickly a corpus grows.
3. **Audit video alt text.** Section 4 measured alt text for images only,
   but the [`app.bsky.embed.video`](https://bsky.network/docs/advanced-guides/posts)
   lexicon has an `alt` field too. Inspect a video post's embed view with
   `describe_embed()`-style code (try `str(post$embed, max.level = 2)`)
   to find where `alt` lives, then compute the panel's video alt-text
   provision rate and compare it to the image rate.
4. **Alt-text rates across communities.** Pick two communities — two
   starter packs, or two of Part 03's network clusters — and sample 10–20
   accounts from each. Compute per-community alt-text provision rates
   (report the image counts alongside the rates, since small accounts make
   noisy estimates). Do communities differ more than the accounts within
   them?
5. **Link-card domain ecology over time.** Raise `POSTS_PER_ACCOUNT` for
   the two big news accounts to 400–500, bucket their link-card posts by
   month using the `created_at` column (`floor_date(ymd_hms(created_at),
   "month")` from lubridate), and plot each account's own-domain share
   per month. Is Bluesky becoming more or less of a pure distribution
   channel for them?
6. **Validate the aspect-ratio genre guesses.** Section 3 claimed aspect
   ratios proxy for image genre. Hand-label the 12 thumbnails in
   `data/images` (screenshot / photograph / chart / promotional graphic),
   then check the labels against each image's aspect ratio in the
   manifest. Where does the cheap proxy fail, and would CLIP's zero-shot
   labels from Section 7 have done better?

## Research project ideas

**1. What moves accessibility norms? Alt text as a natural experiment.**
*Question:* what actually changes alt-text provision — platform nudges
(the require-alt-text setting, badging of undescribed images), community
enforcement (the stated "no alt text, no repost" norm), or tooling
defaults (cross-posting schedulers that silently drop descriptions)?
*Data:* a systematic sample of accounts stratified by join cohort and
community (Part 03's clusters), with each account's image posts
collected over its full tenure. *Method:* measure per-account provision
rates and description lengths over time; use the event-study designs of
Part 05 around datable shocks (a client adding alt-text badges, a
high-profile norm campaign) to separate platform effects from community
ones. Gleason et al. (2019) supplies both the Twitter baseline and the
audit methodology; Bluesky supplies the variation in design and norms
that Twitter lacked. *Expected challenge:* attributing posts to tooling
is hard — posts do not reliably expose which client created them — so
scheduler use must be inferred indirectly (posting-time regularity,
simultaneous cross-platform publication), and that inference needs
validation.

**2. Visual framing of a contested topic.** *Question:* when different
communities post about the same event — a protest, an election, a
climate disaster — do they *show* it differently, not just describe it
differently? *Data:* images attached to topical posts collected with the
search and snowball machinery of Part 02, joined to community labels from
Part 03's network clustering. *Method:* embed every image with CLIP;
develop a framing codebook from a hand-coded sample (crowd-as-voice vs.
confrontation-with-police; podium portrait vs. unflattering candid);
apply it at scale via zero-shot classification; compare frame prevalence
across communities and across Part 05's event windows. Highfield & Leaver
(2016) lay out the methodological agenda. *Expected challenge:*
validation. Zero-shot labels must be checked against human coders before
any prevalence claim, and CLIP inherits documented demographic and
cultural biases from its web-scraped training data that can
systematically distort exactly the framing categories you care about.

**3. Multimodal text–image (dis)agreement.** *Question:* on which posts do
the words and the pixels tell different stories, and is that divergence a
usable signal — for sarcasm, for decorative imagery, or for the
out-of-context images that drive much visual misinformation? *Data:* the
full multimodal bundle each image post provides — post text, image
pixels, and alt text as a third, author-written channel. *Method:*
compute CLIP cosine similarities between all three channels per post;
characterize the low-agreement tail with hand coding; test whether
mismatch predicts independently identified miscontextualized images.
*Expected challenge:* low similarity is not deception — jokes,
abstractions, and decorative images all score low — so the design lives
or dies on a labeled set of genuinely miscontextualized examples against
which the mismatch signal can be evaluated.
